title: They reject as absurd infinite decrees about connections of possibles (Rutherford, Voetius); so Strang and Twisse
source_text: XXXVIII. Etenim absurdam putant sententiam eorum qui infinita decreta Deo tribuunt de connexionibus contingentibus cujuscunque possibilis cum altero possibili, etiam in iis in quibus nullus ordo, subordinatio, aut cohaerentia apparet. Quasi Deus decrevisset quaecunque futura essent in infinitis mundis a se creabilibus, suppositis infinitis diversis conditionibus. Quae est sententia jamjam ex Samuele Retorforti, & Thesibus Voetii relata: quam expresse rejicit Strangius, Tractatu de Voluntate & Actionibus Dei circa peccatum, lib. 1. cap. 5. & lib. 3. cap. 13. Et Tuissus quoque in dissertatione de scientia Media, lib. 3. pag. 472.
pass_a_gloss: XXXVIII. For they think absurd the opinion of those who attribute to God infinite decrees concerning the contingent connections of any possible with another possible, even in those in which no order, subordination, or coherence appears. As if God had decreed whatever things would be future in infinite worlds creatable by him, infinite diverse conditions being supposed. Which is the opinion just now related from Samuel Rutherford, and the Theses of Voetius: which Strang expressly rejects, in the Treatise on the Will and Actions of God about sin, book 1, chap. 5, and book 3, chap. 13. And Twisse also in the dissertation on middle Knowledge, book 3, page 472.
pass_b_english: They consider absurd the view of those who ascribe to God countless decrees about contingent connections between any one possible thing and another. This includes cases where no order, subordination or coherence appears. It is as though God had decreed whatever would happen in the countless worlds he could create, under countless different conditions.

This is the view just reported from Samuel Rutherford and from Voetius's theses. John Strang expressly rejects it in his treatise On the Will and Actions of God concerning Sin, book 1, chapter 5, and book 3, chapter 13. So does Twisse in his dissertation on middle knowledge, book 3, page 472.

lemmas.latin: in infinitis mundis a se creabilibus
lemmas.gloss: in infinite worlds creatable by him

choices.why: God's decree; 'decree' is kept throughout, with 'decreed' for decrevit.

pass_b_revision.reason: Strangius misidentified as William Strang (1588-1645). Le Blanc's 'Strangius' is Joannes Strangius, John Strang of Glasgow (1584-1654), author of De voluntate et actionibus Dei circa peccatum (Amsterdam, 1657), as Le Blanc himself names him ('Joanne Strangio', De Decretis Pars Secunda XIX) and as the book renders him elsewhere (§§1776-1782, 1862, 1928-1937, 2039, 2054-2055). Name and note corrected; no other change.
